Genome Biology.title: G-quadruplex profiling using single-cell CUT&Tag offers insight into the epigenetic landscape of the developing mouse brain
Genome Biology.abstract: Background G-quadruplexes (G4s) are non-canonical DNA structures that have gained increasing attention for their potential roles in gene regulation and role in neurodegenerative diseases and cancer. Despite their biological significance, G4 structures have not been studied systematically across tissues and cell types. Results In this study, we employ G4 single-cell CUT&Tag (G4 scCUT&Tag) to characterize G4 landscapes in postnatal mouse brain cells, leveraging single-cell analytical approaches commonly used in scRNA-Seq and scATAC-Seq datasets. Using conventional single-cell omics workflows to process and explore our data, we distinguish distinct cell lineages based on G4 heterogeneity and establish that a subset of lineage-specific genes show unique promoter G4s. Multi-omics integration with scRNA-Seq gene expression profiles, using both a covariance-based technique (canonical correlation analysis) and a transfer learning-based approach, enables more accurate cell-type annotation. These integrations not only reveal correlations between G4 signal and gene expression, but demonstrate that G4 scCUT&Tag enables detailed examination of G4 heterogeneity in complex tissues and supports integrative analysis of G4 profiles with other omics layers, offering new insights into the epigenomic landscapes of the developing brain. Conclusions Our findings establish G4 scCUT&Tag as a framework for investigating the cellular heterogeneity of G4 landscapes in complex tissues and provide a basis for exploring their relationships with gene regulation and other layers of chromatin organization.

Genome Biology.title: Structure-guided engineering of eukaryotic Fanzor-ωRNA system enhances in vivo gene editing for dystrophin restoration in a Duchenne mouse model
Genome Biology.abstract: Background Eukaryotic Fanzor (Fz) proteins are compact RNA-guided endonucleases homologous to prokaryotic TnpB/Cas12, offering theoretical advantages for single AAV delivery. However, their low editing efficiency and poorly defined specificity in mammals have hindered therapeutic development. Results Here, we perform structure-guided engineering of Spizellomyces punctatus Fanzor1 nuclease (SpuFz1) to enhance its utility for in vivo genome editing and identify several Fanzor variants whose efficiencies are comparable or only slightly lower than widely-used miniature enAsCas12f1 and large-sized SpCas9. We demonstrate that catalytically dead dSpuFz1-v4.2 can be repurposed for CRISPRa-mediated transcriptional activation in a proof-of-concept manner. Genome-wide PEM-seq in mice reveal low translocation frequencies (below 0.05%, much lower than the background threshold set by the PEM-seq protocol), with no detected events attributable to off-target editing. GUIDE-seq analysis also confirms genome-wide low off-target profile for SpuFz1-v4.2 in human cells, with small amounts of off-target editing due to 3’ terminal sequence tolerability. Embryonic mRNA injection efficiently generates mutant mice. Crucially, single AAV9 delivery of SpuFz1-v4.2 in a humanized Duchenne muscular dystrophy model induces targeted exon skipping, restores dystrophin expression to ~ 10% of wild-type levels, and improves muscle contractile force. Conclusions Structure-guided optimization overcomes the activity barrier of eukaryotic Fanzors while maintaining low off-target effect. The engineered SpuFz1-v4.2 retains the hypercompact size necessary for single AAV packaging, establishing a robust platform for in vivo gene editing. This work positions Fanzor by a preliminary proof-of-concept therapeutic study as a viable, miniature alternative to CRISPR-Cas systems for genetic disease intervention and functional genomics.

Briefings in Bioinformatics.title: HGMetaADR: a multimodal heterogeneous graph meta-learning framework for generalized adverse drug reaction prediction
Briefings in Bioinformatics.abstract: AbstractEarly identification of adverse drug reactions (ADRs), which refer to harmful or unintended responses to medications taken at normal doses, is crucial for reducing clinical trial failures and associated economic costs. However, existing ADR datasets often exhibit a long-tailed label distribution and lack sufficient training examples for rare side effects, making it difficult for vanilla supervised learning models to generalize to underrepresented classes. To address these issues, we propose HGMetaADR, a novel heterogeneous graph-based meta-learning framework for ADR prediction. Built upon a multimodal biomedical knowledge graph, this approach integrates complementary drug-related data, including molecular structures, protein sequences, side effects, and therapeutic indications. It employs a hierarchical attention mechanism to capture semantic dependencies across heterogeneous entities and adopts a model-agnostic meta-learning strategy to enhance adaptation to small-sample classes. We evaluate HGMetaADR under three scenarios—few-shot, zero-shot, and majority—to simulate real-world conditions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that HGMetaADR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Furthermore, ablation studies and pathway enrichment analyses reveal the underlying biological mechanisms linking protein targets, therapeutic indications, and side effects, thereby validating the effectiveness of incorporating heterogeneous biomedical knowledge into ADR modeling.

Briefings in Bioinformatics.title: Surrogate-guided self-play Monte Carlo tree search for antimicrobial peptide sequence optimization and in vitro antibacterial assessment
Briefings in Bioinformatics.abstract: AbstractThe rapid emergence of multidrug-resistant pathogens necessitates the development of novel therapeutic agents, yet the de novo design of antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) is challenged by the vast combinatorial search space and the difficulty of balancing efficacy with toxicity. To address these limitations, we introduce a reinforcement learning framework that employs surrogate-guided self-play Monte Carlo tree search to explore the peptide landscape. By integrating surrogate models for predicted antimicrobial activity, HemoDL-predicted hemolytic propensity, and ESMFold structural confidence, the system performs multi-property computational optimization and candidate prioritization. In silico analysis demonstrated that the optimized peptides adopt amphipathic α-helical structures with high predicted folding confidence and possess favorable docking scores against Staphylococcus aureus resistance targets, including PBP2a and MurA. To assess the biological relevance of the computationally prioritized candidates, 16 peptides were synthesized and evaluated by agar dilution against a 37-strain bacterial panel over a concentration range of 0.25–64 μg/ml. AMP2, AMP7, and AMP9 achieved complete inhibition of at least one tested strain, corresponding to 3 of 16 synthesized candidates (18.75%). AMP12 and AMP13 showed partial growth reduction without complete inhibition within the tested range, whereas the remaining 11 candidates showed no complete inhibition. These findings quantify the current gap between surrogate-defined computational enrichment and assay-specific antibacterial activity. The strain-dependent experimental outcomes further indicate that surrogate, docking, and structural scores do not fully capture all determinants of antibacterial efficacy. The experimental assessment was limited to bacterial agar-dilution activity; mammalian-cell cytotoxicity, wet-lab hemolysis, and peptide-stability assays were not performed. In conclusion, this study establishes a computational framework for the design of bioactive peptides and provides structural insights for bridging the gap between deep learning predictions and experimental outcomes.

Briefings in Bioinformatics.title: GLAlign integrates single-cell multi-omics data via global manifold and local marker gene alignment
Briefings in Bioinformatics.abstract: AbstractIntegrating heterogeneous single-cell multi-omics datasets remains challenging because different modalities are measured in distinct feature spaces and lack cell level pairing. Existing manifold alignment or feature conversion framework are often affected by weak cross-modality associations, geometric ambiguity, and overcorrection. Here we present GLAlign (Global manifold and Local marker gene Alignment), an optimization framework that jointly leverages global manifold structure and local marker gene information to integrate single-cell multi-omics data. GLAlign learns a shared latent space through a global objective comprising maximum mean discrepancy, distortion, and penalty terms, together with a local contrastive triplet loss guided by cross-modality marker gene overlap between independently inferred clusters. We demonstrate GLAlign’s methodological contribution in extending the manifold alignment by biologically informed prior to ensure geometrically plausible and biologically correct alignments without requiring paired cells or manual cell type annotations. We evaluated GLAlign on simulated data and real datasets spanning PBMC scRNA-seq/scATAC-seq, mouse brain SNARE-seq, single-donor and multi-batch CITE-seq, and NCI-N87 scDNA-seq/scRNA-seq integration. Across the evaluated datasets, GLAlign achieved strong modality mixing and biological conservation, remained stable under moderate cell type imbalance and variations in clustering and marker information, and supported cross-modality label transfer and paired cell recovery. These results demonstrate that biologically structured coupling of global and local alignment provides an interpretable framework for heterogeneous single-cell multi-omics integration. GLAlign is freely available at https://github.com/Bateer-Bio/GLAlign.

Briefings in Bioinformatics.title: Biosemantic graph transfer learning for cross-patient cell type annotation and cell–cell interaction analysis in tumor single-cell RNA sequencing
Briefings in Bioinformatics.abstract: AbstractThe exploration of cellular heterogeneity within the tumor microenvironment (TME) via single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) is essential for understanding cancer progression and response to therapy. Current scRNA-seq approaches, however, lack spatial context and rely on incomplete datasets of ligand–receptor interactions, limiting accurate cell type annotation and cell–cell communication inference. This study addresses these challenges using a novel graph neural network model that enhances cell-type prediction and cell-interaction analysis. Our study utilized a dataset consisting of 49 024 cells from 19 patients across three cancer types: leukemia, breast invasive carcinoma, and colorectal cancer. The proposed scGSL model demonstrated robust performance, achieving an average accuracy of 84.83%, precision of 86.23%, recall of 81.51%, and an F1 score of 80.92% across all datasets. These metrics represent a significant enhancement over existing methods, which typically exhibit lower performance metrics. Additionally, by reviewing existing literature on gene interactions within the TME, the scGSL model proves to robustly identify biologically meaningful gene interactions in an unsupervised manner, validated by significant expression differences in key gene pairs across various cancers. The source code and data used in this study can be found at https://github.com/LiYuechao1998/scGSL.

Microbiology Spectrum.abstract: Programmed -1 ribosomal frameshifting (-1PRF) is essential for the balanced expression of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) proteins and efficient viral replication, yet how host factors modulate this process remains incompletely understood. Here, we identify the host RNA-binding protein La-related protein 6 (LARP6) as a host regulator of this mechanism. Structural analysis and mutational dissection of the SARS-CoV-2 frameshifting element reveal that a three-stem-loop pseudoknot downstream of the slippery sequence is critical for efficient -1PRF. Using RNA pulldown and mass spectrometry, we identify LARP6 as a host factor that associates with the -1PRF pseudoknot. LARP6 associates with the viral RNA in a pseudoknot-dependent manner through multiple RNA-binding domains, and both loss- and restore-of-function analyses demonstrate that LARP6 promotes -1PRF efficiency. Mechanistically, LARP6 associates with ribosomal components in an mRNA-dependent manner, and changes in LARP6 expression are accompanied by corresponding changes in ribosome-associated RNA occupancy at the frameshifting region, consistent with a potential role in modulating ribosomal pausing. In a SARS-CoV-2 luciferase replicon, LARP6 overexpression increased RdRp protein levels, providing additional support for LARP6-mediated promotion of -1PRF in a viral genomic context. Together, our findings identify LARP6 as a host regulator of SARS-CoV-2 -1PRF and suggest that LARP6 may regulate frameshifting through its association with the viral pseudoknot and ribosomes.IMPORTANCESevere acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) relies on programmed -1 ribosomal frameshifting (-1PRF) to regulate the production of viral replicase proteins, making this process an important point of control in the viral life cycle. Although the viral RNA structures that promote -1PRF have been extensively studied, how host factors contribute to this process remains less well understood. Our study identifies LARP6 as a host protein associated with the SARS-CoV-2 -1PRF pseudoknot and reveals a potential link between LARP6-viral RNA interaction and ribosome behavior at the frameshifting site. These findings expand the current understanding of -1PRF regulation beyond viral RNA structures and suggest that host RNA-binding proteins may contribute to the control of viral gene expression by interacting with structured RNA elements. This work highlights the interaction of host RNA-binding proteins with viral RNA structures as a potentially important layer of translational regulation in coronaviruses.

PLOS Computational Biology.title: Entangled stoichiometric objectives shape microbial catabolism
PLOS Computational Biology.abstract: by Maaike Remeijer, Frank J. Bruggeman The understanding of fundamental relationships between energetic and biosynthetic parameters of catabolism and anabolism is a central challenge in microbiology. The large diversity of microbial metabolisms can be compared on the basis of our current definitions of catabolism and anabolism. Catabolism has two functions: synthesising charged energy carriers and carbon precursors. Energy carriers, however, are also involved in precursor synthesis, complicating the analysis. We introduce an unbiased method to quantify stoichiometric relationships between catabolism and anabolism in genome-scale metabolic models. We compare catabolic strategies across diverse (heterotrophic) microbial species and growth conditions, focusing on states of maximal biomass yield per unit of energy source. Catabolic networks turn out to vary greatly, due to variation in the energy and carbon source for growth and the requirement to make suitable precursors for anabolism. We find that the ATP requirement for 1 gram biomass ranges between 72.8 and 148.0 mmol, precursor sets range between 4 and 14 in size, and acetyl-CoA is the only universal precursor across species. An important varying factor is the amount of ATP that is produced or consumed during precursor synthesis. This causes the remaining ATP demand, which is produced in catabolism, to vary. We conclude that the diversity of heterotrophic catabolism results from entanglement between charging of energy carriers and precursor synthesis. The state of maximal energetic efficiency is reached by maximizing the yield of charged energy carriers during precursor synthesis and simultaneously minimizing the demand for charged energy carriers in the conversion of precursors into macromolecules. Our formal analysis of catabolic diversity using a rigorous definition of catabolism’s two functions shows that microbial metabolism cannot be simplified in this manner; it rather shows that these two functions are intertwined due to the precise biochemistry.

PLOS Computational Biology.title: Handshake: Partner-specific protein-protein binding site prediction at scale using ProstT5 and cross-chain attention
PLOS Computational Biology.abstract: by Nurit Haspel Partner-specific protein-protein binding site prediction, identifying which residues of a protein form the interface when bound to a specific partner, remains a challenging task with significant implications for drug discovery and understanding of protein structure and function. Existing computational methods are limited by small training datasets, inconsistent redundancy filtering, and reliance on three-dimensional structural information at test time. Here we present a sequence-only, partner-specific protein-protein interface predictor called HandShake. It combines ProstT5, a protein language model pre-trained on structural data, with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), a cross-chain attention mechanism and a contact supervision head. Our method can detect both binding interfaces and pairwise contact matrices. We trained our model on very large datasets of non-redundant protein-protein pairs derived from the PPInterface dataset, the most comprehensive structural protein-protein database to date, and evaluated it on systematically filtered benchmarks at four redundancy thresholds (30%–90% sequence identity). We demonstrate that sequence redundancy inflates reported AUROC by up to 0.079 and MCC by up to 0.145 on identical models, representing a substantial methodological confound in the field. Even at 30% redundancy threshold, our results (AUROC = 0.811, MCC = 0.367, F1 = 0.45) exceed the best published sequence-only result on this convention. Our method also achieves comparable performance to existing partner-specific methods that use explicit structural information. The comprehensive training and evaluation dataset, in addition to the systematic redundancy inflation, can help gain insight into protein-protein interactions and the abilities and limitations of current detection methods.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: DIANA-miRGen v5: TSS characterization and transcriptional regulation of miRNAs in human and mouse.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: Characterizing microRNA transcriptional regulation is challenging because primary microRNA transcripts undergo rapid nuclear processing, leaving full-length molecules poorly represented in conventional transcriptomic data. DIANA-miRGen v5 addresses this annotation gap by combining Capture Long-read Sequencing (CLS) data, generated within GENCODE to improve non-coding RNA annotation, with GENCODE reference gene and transcript annotations to resolve miRNA host contexts. For human, the database provides experimentally informed, transcript-anchored host and promoter annotations for 1560/1918 pre-miRNA loci (81.3%), represented by 1302 distinct reference transcripts. CLS-derived human transcription start sites (TSSs) are accompanied by overlap information from FANTOM5 CAGE, ENCODE PRO-cap, and RAMPAGE. Transcription factor (TF)-filtered ChIP-Atlas data annotate candidate TF occupancy within windows extending 10 kb upstream and 2 kb downstream of selected host TSSs, yielding 4 901 330 human gene-level host-window overlap records. For mouse, annotations cover 994/1227 loci (81.0%), comprising 785 distinct reference transcripts. Mouse TSSs obtained from CLS include FANTOM5 CAGE overlap information, while ChIP-Atlas analysis yielded 2 378 918 gene-level host-window overlap records. The redesigned interface supports linked gene- and transcript-level exploration, interactive genome visualization, contextual tracks, bulk downloads, and open access through a REST API. DIANA-miRGen v5 is freely available without registration at http://microrna.gr/mirgenv5/.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: Evo2VED: a database of DNA large language model-derived scores for variant interpretation.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: The Evo2 Variant Effect Database (Evo2VED; https://dnallmved.org/) is a publicly accessible resource cataloging precomputed Evo2-derived variant effect scores, defined as allelic score differences, for 6.48 million human variants common in the gnomAD non-Finnish European population. Evo2VED includes scores from the 7B and 40B models under three scoring schemes, alongside annotations of variant function, evolutionary constraint, allele age, and disease associations. It integrates genome-wide association study (GWAS) data from UK Biobank, FinnGen, and the Million Veteran Program. Three complementary modules support variant-level interpretation, regional and region-set exploration, and trait-level analysis through flexible queries, interactive visualizations, and downloadable results. Evo2VED also catalogs associations between Evo2 annotations and per-SNP heritability across thousands of traits from these biobanks. A guided workflow connects GWAS with associated regions and individual variant evidence. Case studies of hypertension and depression illustrate how regional comparisons of Evo2 scores and GWAS signals can guide candidate variant prioritization. Evaluations using massively parallel reporter assays, molecular QTLs, fine-mapping probabilities, and clinical annotations assess associations with Evo2 scores alone and their added value beyond conservation and regulatory annotations. By providing accessible scores, contextual annotations, and comparative analyses, Evo2VED facilitates exploration and application of genomic language model predictions in human genetics research.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: TransCirc 2.0: a multi-species resource for translatable circular RNAs and cognate translation products.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: TransCirc is an evidence-integrated database for evaluating the translation potential of circular RNAs (circRNAs) and their putative products. Here, we present TransCirc 2.0, a major update that expands this resource from a primarily human-focused database to 10 vertebrate species, comprising more than 2.8 million circRNAs and increasing coverage by approximately 10-fold through the integration of standardized full-length circRNA sequences. Within the original multi-evidence framework, we incorporate additional evidence, including translation initiation sites, internal ribosome entry sites, N6-methyladenosine, ribosome/polysome association, and mass spectrometry (MS), together with circRNA-specific open reading frame and sequence-composition annotations. In light of recent advances in AI-based RNA modeling, we further incorporate multiple regulatory features predicted by TranslationAI and LAMAR. The circRNA-encoded proteins are further annotated for degron-associated stability and degradation properties, while MS-supported peptides are evaluated for potential MHC-I presentation. Collectively, these updates establish a cross-species framework linking full-length circRNA sequences with multi-level translation evidence and downstream product annotations, supporting systematic evaluation of circRNA translation potential and putative translation products. TransCirc 2.0 is freely available at https://www.biosino.org/transcirc/.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: ADMETatlas: an online database of peptide ADMET evidence toward peptide therapeutic development.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: Peptide therapeutics are expanding rapidly, yet poor permeability and limited in vivo stability still decide whether a candidate reaches the clinic. Judging these properties is difficult, because one sequence can be studied as different molecular forms or products, and reported values carry different experimental contexts. Despite the continuous accumulation of measurements of peptide absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity (ADMET), few open-access resources keep each value attached to the material tested and its assay context. Herein, we present ADMETatlas, a curated peptide ADMET, safety, and developability database. Currently, ADMETatlas contains 39 641 measurements at 17 measured end points across 37 467 canonical peptide identities, 110 drug products, and 10 computed descriptors. Each measurement retains its value, unit, formal end point, assay context, and primary reference. Peptide identities, molecular forms, and products are cross-linked at the resolution each source supports. In addition to browsing and retrieval, a developability module profiles single candidates and compares several side by side. Applications to GLP-1 receptor agonists and polymyxin B show how route and formulation change the reading of peptide pharmacokinetics. We hope that ADMETatlas will prove useful in evidence-based peptide optimization and condition-aware modeling. ADMETatlas is freely available, without registration, at https://admetatlas.scbdd.com/.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: M2iOR: a quantitative, context-resolved atlas of insect odorant receptor-odorant interactions.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: Olfactory detection in insects relies on interactions between odorant molecules and odorant receptors (ORs) expressed in olfactory sensory neurons. Although numerous studies have characterized insect OR-ligand interactions, these data remain scattered across the literature and heterogeneous in terms of species, experimental systems, and reporting standards, limiting their systematic analysis. Here, we present the Molecule to Insect Odorant Receptor database (M2iOR, https://m2ior.chemsensim.fr/), a curated, publicly accessible resource designed to centralize and standardize odorant-receptor interaction data. In its current release, M2iOR compiles 35 891 bioassay experiments describing 30 348 distinct insect OR-molecule pairs, extracted from 41 peer-reviewed publications and public databases. The resource integrates ligand structures, receptor sequences, species names, mixture information, and detailed experimental metadata. M2iOR provides flexible query tools allowing users to retrieve activity profiles for individual molecules or compound sets, and identify agonists and nonagonists for specific insect ORs, enabling comparative analyses across receptors, species, or bioassay systems. Advanced filtering based on curated metadata and batch search functionality support high-throughput analyses. For each query, users can visualize and download a curated aggregation of experimental results, including a binarized combinatorial representation of olfactory coding suitable for downstream computational studies. M2iOR provides a comprehensive framework for data-driven research in insect olfaction and comparative chemosensory biology.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: The Biodiversity Cell Atlas database: a curated resource for comparative single-cell genomics across the eukaryotic tree of life.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: Single-cell genomics has transformed the study of cellular diversity, but the resulting atlases are scattered across publications, formats, and annotation standards. Efforts to make these data findable and interoperable have focused largely on aggregating and harmonizing existing model organism datasets. The Biodiversity Cell Atlas database is an open resource that addresses this gap by uniformly (re)processing, curating, and comparing whole-organism single-cell atlases sampled across the eukaryotic tree of life. Starting from raw sequencing data, each dataset is processed through a consistent workflow and enriched with standardized quality-control metrics, metacell-level aggregation, gene co-expression modules, and phylogeny-based orthology and functional annotation, enabling both gene- and cell type-centric exploration within species as well as principled comparisons between them. The portal currently hosts 39 datasets across 33 species spanning 13 eukaryotic phyla, and offers multiple levels of access, from raw and filtered count matrices to normalized, aggregated, and analysis-ready data layers. These are accessible through an interactive web interface (https://portal.biodiversitycellatlas.org) and a documented REST API (https://portal.biodiversitycellatlas.org/api/v1/). All data, code, and infrastructure are continuously released and maintained under open licenses, providing a curated and reusable foundation for comparative single-cell genomics.

mSystems.title: Characterizing gut microbial structural variation reveals strain heterogeneity and metabolic dysfunction in colorectal cancer.
mSystems.abstract: Previous studies investigating gastrointestinal (GI) diseases have primarily focused on the composition, gene expression, and specific strains of gut microbiota. However, the impact of genetic variations, especially structural variations (SVs) in microbial genomes, on the development of GI tumors has been largely overlooked. In this study, we analyzed 1,027 fecal metagenomes from seven data sets and identified 8,278 coverage-defined SVs across 51 bacterial species in the gut microbiomes. We found that SVs were prevalent in the gut microbiota of studied cohorts. Surprisingly, the genetic makeup of SV-based clusters differed significantly between healthy individuals and those with colorectal cancer (CRC), indicating substantial intra-specific diversity within these populations. By integrating taxonomic-SV markers, we achieved optimal accuracy in early CRC detection, and the SVs also displayed regional heterogeneity. Microbial genetic variation provides additional insights into taxonomy and functionality, allowing us to have a more precise understanding of the microbiota associated with CRC. Notably, our study uncovered potential links between microbial SVs and metabolic disorders of CRC, including SV regions that encode glycoside hydrolases associated with disordered carbohydrate metabolism in CRC. We integrated a framework called MicroSVsProfiler to identify and classify SVs in individuals diagnosed with CRC, as well as in healthy controls. Our findings underscore the importance of considering SVs in microbiome studies, especially in the absence of strain-specific differences in abundance. Future research should explore the deeper layer of the microbiota's structural variantome for a better understanding of the occurrence and characteristics of CRC across different stages.IMPORTANCEMost microbiome studies of colorectal cancer focus on which bacterial species are more or less abundant, potentially overlooking genetic differences among strains of the same species. By analyzing 1,027 fecal metagenomes from seven independent cohorts, we show that large-scale changes in bacterial genomes, known as structural variations, provide disease-related information that is not captured by species abundance alone. These strain-level SV signatures distinguished healthy individuals from patients with colorectal cancer, improved early-cancer classification when combined with taxonomic markers, and varied across geographic populations. We also found that cancer-associated structural variations were linked to altered microbial metabolic functions, particularly carbohydrate metabolism and glycoside hydrolases. Together, these findings establish microbial structural variation as a complementary dimension of the gut microbiome and provide a framework for developing more precise, population-aware biomarkers and for investigating how strain-level genetic changes may contribute to metabolic disturbances associated with colorectal cancer.

mSystems.title: TSAR, thermal shift analysis in R, identifies endogenous molecules that interact with HIV-1 capsid hexamers.
mSystems.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Thermal shift assay (TSA) is a versatile biophysical technique for studying protein-ligand interactions in vitro. Here, we report a free, open-source software tool, TSAR (thermal shift analysis in R), to expedite the analysis of TSA data. The TSAR package incorporates multiple workflows that facilitate TSA analyses, returns publication-ready graphics, and includes an optional graphic user interface. The package is available at https://doi.org/10.18129/B9.bioc.TSAR. Applying TSAR, we screened two chemical libraries and found multiple molecules that potentially interact in vitro with the capsid protein (CA) of human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1). First, a library of vitamins exemplifies the different graphic outputs of TSAR. Since HIV-1 CA hexamers (CAHEX) interact with host-derived acids like inositol hexaphosphate or dNTPs, a second library was screened containing 96 organic, acidic metabolites; multiple anionic ligands caused a change in melting temperature (∆Tm) for CAHEX. Subsequent investigation of these interactions included biolayer interferometry, antiviral activity against VSV-G-pseudotyped HIV-1, and endogenous reverse transcriptase assays that were used to validate and investigate the biological impact of these native ligands that thermally stabilize CAHEX. One compound hit, gallic acid, exhibited anti-HIV-1 activity as previously reported, and we show that it interacts with CAHEX by a suggested novel mechanism. This paper aims to showcase examples of TSA screens and follow-up studies to validate the biological relevance of the hits. Thus, the TSAR package facilitated quick analysis of TSA data from multiple libraries to help identify a biologically relevant hit, gallic acid, as a molecule that can inhibit HIV-1 replication by targeting CAHEX. [IMPORTANCE] The TSAR package is freely available (AGPL-3) and is designed for both experienced and new R users, having command-line code for handling large and challenging datasets while also including an optional graphic user interface that enables easy use by non-programmers. This thermal shift assay (TSA) analysis program is written in R, a free and open-source language; TSAR simplifies TSA analysis while maintaining diverse visualization options for small-to-large libraries and multidimensional analysis. Additionally, we report multiple endogenous metabolites that potentially interact with the HIV-1 capsid protein hexamers (CAHEX) in vitro, including folic acid, gallic acid, and multiple others, primarily from the tricarboxylic acid cycle. Various methods validate gallic acid interactions with CAHEX, leading to a suggested novel mechanism of action, and in line with previous reports, this metabolite may have potential for natural-based treatments of HIV-1.

mSphere.title: H2-O deficiency is associated with altered intestinal bacterial communities and differential IgG binding.
mSphere.abstract: The non-classical major histocompatibility complex class II (MHCII) molecule H2-O regulates peptide loading by inhibiting H2-M, thereby restricting the repertoire of high-affinity peptides presented to CD4+ T cells. H2-O deficiency enhances protective immunoglobulin G (IgG) responses against pathogens, including retroviruses and Staphylococcus aureus, and promotes the generation of IgG specific for the commensal bacterium Staphylococcus xylosus. Whether these expanded antibody responses influence intestinal microbial communities is unknown. Here, using gnotobiotic mouse models, we demonstrate that H2-O shapes the gut bacterial composition to a limited but significant extent. H2-O deficiency was associated with increased serum IgG reactivity against commensal microbial antigens (Ags). Sequencing antibody-coated bacteria revealed distinct populations between H2-O-deficient and H2-O-sufficient mice within the IgG-coated, but not IgA-coated, fractions. Together, these findings identify an association between H2-O genotype and microbiome composition and reveal differential IgG, but not IgA, binding to intestinal bacterial communities. These results expand current understanding of how Ag presentation pathways influence host-microbiome interactions and suggest a potential relationship between regulation of the MHCII peptidome, IgG responses, and commensal ecology.IMPORTANCEOur findings demonstrate that the absence of H2-O not only promotes protective IgG responses against retroviruses and Staphylococcus aureus but also is associated with altered intestinal IgG binding patterns and differences in gut microbiome composition.

Journal of Virology.title: CHD4 promotes hepatitis B virus transcription by facilitating RNA polymerase II recruitment to cccDNA.
Journal of Virology.abstract: Chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection remains a major global health burden, largely due to the persistence of covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA), which serves as the template for viral transcription. Although host factors involved in regulating cccDNA transcription have been increasingly recognized, the molecular mechanisms controlling HBV minichromosome activity remain incompletely understood. Chromodomain helicase DNA-binding protein 4 (CHD4), the catalytic component of the nucleosome remodeling and deacetylase (NuRD) complex, is a key regulator of chromatin remodeling and transcriptional regulation. In this study, we demonstrate that CHD4 facilitates efficient HBV transcription. Depletion of CHD4 in HBV-infected hepatoma cells markedly reduced viral RNA levels and antigen production without affecting HBV uptake, nuclear import, cccDNA establishment, or cccDNA stability. Mechanistically, CHD4 was recruited to HBV cccDNA and promoted the occupancy of RNA polymerase II (RNA Pol II) on the viral minichromosome. Loss of CHD4 impaired RNA Pol II recruitment to cccDNA, resulting in reduced viral transcription. Furthermore, domain mapping identified the CT2 region of CHD4 as essential for its interaction with RNA Pol II. Collectively, our findings reveal a previously unrecognized role of CHD4 in regulating HBV cccDNA transcription and establish CHD4-mediated RNA Pol II recruitment as a critical mechanism controlling HBV gene expression.IMPORTANCEHepatitis B virus (HBV) infection affects hundreds of millions of people worldwide and can lead to severe liver diseases, including cirrhosis and liver cancer. A major challenge in curing HBV infection is the persistence of a stable viral DNA structure inside infected liver cells that continuously produces viral components. Understanding how this viral DNA is controlled by host cells is essential for developing new therapeutic strategies. In this study, we identified chromodomain helicase DNA-binding protein 4 (CHD4) as a host factor that supports HBV gene production by helping the virus recruit the cellular machinery required for viral RNA synthesis. Our findings reveal a previously unrecognized mechanism by which human liver cells regulate HBV persistence and provide new insights into virus-host interactions that may guide future approaches to achieve durable HBV control.

Journal of Virology.title: Neuropsychiatric long COVID is associated with altered SARS-CoV-2-specific cellular-humoral coordination and diminished EBV-specific humoral immunity up to 12 months post-COVID-19 symptom onset.
Journal of Virology.abstract: Long COVID is a chronic multisystemic condition estimated to affect approximately 400 million people worldwide. Although underlying mechanisms remain elusive, persistent SARS-CoV-2 reservoirs and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) reactivation have been implicated. We compared SARS-CoV-2- and EBV-specific cellular and humoral immunity between 27 long COVID individuals with ≥2 neuropsychiatric symptoms and 27 matched recovered participants at 3-6 months post-COVID-19 symptom onset (PSO). Peripheral blood mononuclear cells were assessed for IFN-γ, IL-2, TNF, and granzyme B T-cell responses against SARS-CoV-2, EBV, and HCMV. Sera were evaluated for neutralizing activity against live ancestral SARS-CoV-2 and EBV, while EBV reactivation was assessed by anti-early antigen-diffuse IgG and anti-viral capsid antigen (VCA) IgM. We observed no significant differences in SARS-CoV-2-, EBV-, or HCMV-specific Th1-type/cytotoxic T-cell responses or live virus neutralization between long COVID and recovered groups at 3-6 months PSO. Although SARS-CoV-2-specific IFN-γ and IL-2 T-cell responses correlated with serological neutralizing capacity in recovered participants, no such associations were observed in the long COVID group, suggesting altered coordination between cellular and humoral immunity. EBV reactivation was only detected in one neuropsychiatric long COVID participant. However, EBV anti-VCA IgG antibody levels were significantly diminished in long COVID participants at 3-6 months PSO. Reports of fatigue at 12 months PSO were also associated with reduced EBV neutralizing capacity at 3-6 months PSO. Diminished EBV-specific humoral immunity and dysregulated coordination between SARS-CoV-2-specific cellular and humoral immunity may thus represent potential prognostic markers for neuropsychiatric long COVID development and fatigue up to 12 months PSO.IMPORTANCEWe performed a comprehensive analysis of cellular and humoral immune responses to SARS-CoV-2, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), and human cytomegalovirus in individuals with neuropsychiatric long COVID, a subgroup that remains poorly characterized. Although no differences in virus-specific Th1-type or cytotoxic T-cell immunity were observed between individuals with long COVID and recovered individuals, altered coordination between SARS-CoV-2-specific T-cell and neutralizing humoral immunity was observed in the long COVID group at 3-6 months post-COVID-19 symptom onset (PSO). Diminished EBV-specific humoral immunity was also associated with neuropsychiatric long COVID and fatigue up to 12 months PSO. Together, these findings suggest that altered SARS-CoV-2-specific cellular-humoral immune coordination and diminished EBV-specific humoral immunity may contribute to the development or persistence of neuropsychiatric long COVID and highlight a promising future direction for mechanistic studies.CLINICAL TRIALSThis study is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov as NCT05125510.

Journal of Virology.title: A rotavirus-vectored bivalent vaccine elicits protective immunity against bovine coronavirus and rotavirus.
Journal of Virology.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Bovine rotavirus (BRV) and bovine coronavirus (BCoV) are major causes of neonatal calf diarrhea and frequently occur as co-infections. Here, we engineered the Lanzhou lamb rotavirus vaccine strain LLR to express either the N-terminal domain (NTD) or the C-terminal domain (CTD) of the BCoV spike S1 subunit from a modified genome segment 8. The resulting viruses, rLLR-GSG-P2A-BCoV NTD and rLLR-GSG-P2A-BCoV CTD, replicated efficiently in cell culture, stably retained the inserted sequences through serial passage, and expressed the corresponding BCoV antigens. In a mouse model, oral inoculation of neonatal mice induced systemic antibody responses against both RV and BCoV. Maternal immunization in mice protected suckling mice against RV challenge and conferred partial protection against BCoV-associated diarrhea. In pregnant cows, intramuscular immunization elicited RV- and BCoV-specific serum antibodies, and the rLLR-GSG-P2A-BCoV CTD immunization modestly increased neutralizing antibody titers in colostrum. These findings establish the LLR strain as a genetically stable vector for the delivery of heterologous coronavirus antigens and support further evaluation of rotavirus-vectored vaccines for controlling viral coinfections that contribute to neonatal calf diarrhea. [IMPORTANCE] Neonatal calf diarrhea is frequently caused by more than one enteric pathogen, yet most vaccines target individual agents. We developed recombinant rotaviruses that express neutralizing-antibody targets from the bovine coronavirus spike protein. The vaccine candidates rLLR-GSG-P2A-BCoV CTD maintained efficient replication and stable antigen expression, induced antibodies against both viruses in mice, and increased neutralizing activity in the serum and colostrum of immunized cows. This study provides proof of concept for using a licensed rotavirus vaccine backbone as a bivalent platform against two major viral causes of calf diarrhea and identifies a strategy that could be adapted to other polymicrobial enteric diseases.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Predominance of viral core functions over auxiliary metabolism among carbohydrate-active enzymes annotated in the global soil virosphere.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Soil viruses are increasingly recognized as components of microbial communities with the potential to alter ecosystem functioning, yet the frequency and functional distribution of virus-encoded metabolic genes in soils remain poorly understood. Here, the Global Soil Virus Atlas gene catalog, comprising 1,432,147 viral genes from 1,223 samples across 12 ecosystem types, was searched against KEGG, Pfam, and CAZy for functions related to carbon cycling, nitrogen cycling, and antimicrobial resistance. Annotations associated with host entry or cell-wall lysis were separated from putative auxiliary metabolic functions. Of 5,020 initial gene-level functional annotations across the three categories, 3,322 (66.2%) were classified as peptidoglycanases. Their exclusion left 1,698 genes (0.14% of the gene catalog restricted to contigs ≥10 kb), and carbon-cycling functions represented 96.7% of the enzyme-resolved annotations. Chitinase-associated genes formed the largest carbon category, but 78.0% belonged to GH19, a family containing both chitinases and phage endolysins. Among GH19 genes on contigs encoding detectable holins or spanins, 84.2% occurred within three genes of these lysis components, a distribution comparable to that of canonical phage lysozymes. Across six matched metagenomic studies, estimated viral contributions to the targeted functions ranged from 0.00% to 8.45% (mean: 2.27%). Two of the three estimates exceeding 2% were GH19-associated chitinase estimates from rhizosphere soils and were therefore treated as upper estimates. Thus, the putative soil viral metabolic inventory was sparse and concentrated in carbon-degradation functions, whereas much of the initial carbohydrate-active enzyme signal reflected core viral lysis functions rather than auxiliary metabolism. [IMPORTANCE] Soil microorganisms drive decomposition and nutrient cycling, and the viruses that infect them may alter these processes by carrying genes that affect host metabolism. However, genes annotated as carbohydrate-degradation enzymes may instead help viruses enter cells or break host cell walls when new virus particles are released. In a worldwide catalog of soil viruses, approximately two-thirds of the initial functional assignments represented these infection or release activities. After their removal, putative viral auxiliary metabolic genes were uncommon and concentrated mainly in carbon degradation. Genes potentially involved in chitin degradation were most frequent, but many occurred near viral genes used to break host cells; their estimated contribution should therefore be viewed as an upper limit. Distinguishing core viral functions from host metabolic modification is essential to avoid overestimating viral contributions to soil processes and to identify the strongest candidates for experimental testing.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Rhodococcus rhodnii boosts host tolerance and mitigates virulence of Serratia species in Rhodnius prolixus.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: Insects contend with myriad microbes throughout their lives. These microbial interactions, ranging from beneficial to pathogenic, have important consequences for the insect host, and simultaneous infection with multiple microbes is the norm. We are increasingly aware of how within-host interactions between the endogenous microbiota and invading pathogens can influence host infection outcomes. In this study, we examined how symbiont-pathogen interactions influence pathogen infection in the insect Rhodnius prolixus and how virulence can vary drastically with the context of infection, including cases where the endogenous microbiota is disrupted. Leveraging our ability to rear symbiont-free, or aposymbiotic, individuals, we first challenged symbiotic and aposymbiotic R. prolixus with three Serratia strains of varying virulence (two virulent Serratia marcescens strains and one avirulent Serratia ureilytica strain). We further altered the context of infection by varying the order of symbiont and pathogen colonization, as well as the method of inoculation (i.e., ingestion vs injection). Within R. prolixus, we showed a strong mitigating effect on virulence with the presence of Rhodococcus rhodnii, a well-established R. prolixus symbiont, despite high Serratia burdens. Virulence varied not only by Serratia strain but also by host species, with R. prolixus being particularly susceptible to infection among the four insect species tested. Our findings corroborate the importance of context in determining pathogen virulence, with symbiont presence, in particular, playing a key role in the outcome of pathogen infection for R. prolixus.IMPORTANCEThroughout their lives, insects encounter many bacteria, some beneficial and some detrimental. Increasingly, we are aware of how resident bacteria in the insect gut impact the ability of pathogenic microbes to establish and cause harm. Understanding the factors that underlie the specificity of these interactions is important in furthering our ability to leverage pathogenic microbes for the control of insect pests. This study focuses on the kissing bug, Rhodnius prolixus, a medically important insect that transmits Chagas disease. We tested the impact of different conditions in determining the virulence of the pathogen Serratia marcescens. Kissing bugs suffered high levels of mortality when infected with Serratia, particularly compared to other insect species. We determined that the presence of a beneficial bacterium (Rhodococcus rhodnii) in the kissing bug mitigated the ill effects of infection with Serratia. Early establishment of the beneficial bacteria was key to maximizing this effect.

Genome Biology and Evolution.title: Evolutionary dynamics of the vertebrate Wnt gene repertoire.
Genome Biology and Evolution.abstract: The Wnt gene family plays a central role in vertebrate development, yet its evolutionary dynamics across lineages remain largely unexplored. Here, we present the most comprehensive analysis of Wnt gene evolution in vertebrates to date, leveraging a large-scale comparative genomics approach of 38,886 Wnt gene sequences mined from 1,961 species. We first investigate overall patterns of gene retention, duplication, and loss, and then focus specifically on the impact of whole-genome duplications (WGDs). We uncover striking variation in Wnt gene repertoire sizes, with ray-finned fishes (Actinopterygii) exhibiting the largest repertoires - even after excluding taxa with recent WGDs. Notably, we identify extreme expansions in polyploid cyprinids, including an octoploid hybrid harbouring 99 Wnt genes, the highest number observed. Unexpectedly elevated Wnt copy numbers in diploid species, such as in the Antarctic lanternfish (Electrona antarctica) and the brook lamprey (Lethenteron reissneri), point to lineage-specific expansions, although the potential adaptive significance of these expansions remains to be tested. Evolutionary rate analyses reveal that certain Wnt clades - especially Wnt8 and Wnt16 - exhibit elevated dN/dS ratios and high birth-death rates, consistent with repeated episodes of relaxed constraint and/or adaptive diversification. Contrary to our expectations, there was no relationship between developmental expression timing and evolutionary rates, suggesting pleiotropic regulation and functional redundancy of Wnt genes. Altogether, our findings reveal widespread variation in Wnt copy number and turnover among lineages, shaped by both genome duplication history and divergent evolutionary trajectories. This work provides a high-resolution framework for understanding the molecular evolution of a key developmental toolkit and highlights candidate genes for future studies of vertebrate eco-morphological diversity.

Trends in Microbiology.title: The microbial glycan landscape instructs natural antibody repertoires
authors: Bahtiyar Yilmaz, Miguel P. Soares, Andrew J. Macpherson
Trends in Microbiology.abstract: The human gut mucosa presents a dynamic glycan landscape, built from host, microbial, and dietary carbohydrates and remodeled throughout life. Gut microbes deploy a vast repertoire of surface glycans that drive immune evasion, lectin signaling, immunomodulation, and ecological competition. Natural antiglycan antibodies, we argue, are not fixed baseline features of humoral immunity but are structured readouts of glycan exposure, founded during early-life colonization and revised thereafter by diet, infection, vaccination, and inflammation. We trace how microbial glycan diversity arises, how specific glycan classes instruct antibody specificity, and how disrupting this glycan-immune dialog drives inflammatory bowel disease, xenosialitis, infection, and allergy. Reframing natural antibodies as ecologically instructed rather than genetically preset identifies the glycan landscape as a lifelong determinant of immune calibration.

PLOS Biology.abstract: by Mahmoud Keshavarzi, Georgia Feltham, Susan Richards, Lyla Parvez, Usha Goswami Neural tracking of slow temporal modulations in speech supports extraction of the prosodic and syllabic structure thought to be critical for language acquisition by Temporal Sampling (TS) theory, yet whether these automatic cortical tracking mechanisms are altered in children with developmental language disorder (DLD) remains unclear. We recorded MEG while children with and without DLD listened to a story, and quantified source-level lagged speech-brain coherence and frequency-specific cortical functional connectivity across bilateral cortical regions. As expected a priori by TS theory, children with DLD showed significantly reduced coherence in the 0.9–2.5 Hz range associated with prosodic information in the story, spanning bilateral auditory and speech-related cortex. The strongest regional group differences were in left supramarginal gyrus (p p = 0.001). In the 2.5–5 Hz range, linked to syllabic-rate modulations in the story, children with DLD showed reduced coherence in right temporal regions (all p < 0.02). Stronger low-frequency speech-brain coherence was associated with better language performance, indicating that individual differences in cortical speech tracking were behaviourally meaningful. No reliable differences were observed at higher modulation rates (5–9 Hz or 12–40 Hz). Exploratory functional connectivity analyses did not reveal network-level group differences that were robust across ROI time-series extraction methods. These findings indicate that atypical low-frequency neural tracking of speech is functionally relevant to language outcomes in DLD.
